newsitem.title: MEXICO: Puzzling execution-style deaths sow fear in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Puzzling execution-style deaths sow fear in Mexico.

text.p: More and more bodies are turning up on the streets of Jalisco state with a bullet in the head, sowing fear among Mexicans.
Since December last year, 23 bodies have been dumped on the streets, many with their limbs tied and an execution-style shot to the head, authorities said.

Local media, however, report more than 70 such killings and point a finger at drug traffickers battling each other and police for control of one of Mexico's busiest smuggling areas. Up to 70 percent of the illegal drugs entering the United States came via Mexico, according to U.S. anti-drug officials.
Tying up enemies and shooting them in the head is widely seen as their killing style of choice. The bodies are often wrapped in plastic. Sometimes they are hacked into bits.
Police are reluctant to blame all the deaths on the increasingly cut-throat narcotics trade, while some Mexicans suspect the killers could in fact be crooked cops.
Jalisco is one of the main centres for Mexican gangs with ties to Colombian cocaine cartels, and it is just north of Michoacan, Mexico's main marijuana- and poppy-growing state.

"I am not going to deny that there have been some people executed," said a state judicial police official who asked to remain anonymous. "In this case we can talk about 60 percent being drug-related."
The remaining 40 percent of deaths are attributable to car-theft rings or personal vendettas, he said.

The spokesman for Jalisco's Attorney General's Office, Teodulo Zepeda, dismissed the idea the state was witnessing a wave of Colombian-style drug murders, and said the killers were trying to make their crimes appear drug-related.

"Some people seeking vengeance against someone very easily can make it look like this kind of execution to mislead the investigagtion," Zepeda told Reuters. "They can't all be executions and revenge by drug traffickers."
So if drugs are not behind the killings, who is? Some police officers single out their own colleagues.

"A lot of people belonging to the police forces, whether state or federal, know the methods, know how to execute," Hector Cordoba Bermudez, former chief of the state's Judicial Police, told Reuters in an interview. "That's what they're doing, so we're not going to tie them to drug trafficking."
